-The letter that is a square closed on every side but the way creation flowS-

Though it is true that no one can surf the surface of surfaces to see before creation - yet perhaps there are deeper allusions among the dangers of causing damage to the text to project your own illusion upon it. 

this is a thought experiment just to help guide you through some of the features of sefaria. there is no pressure to rush any of it, for the nature of the torah, the words of our sages of blessed memory, those who still may live for 120 or even 180, may the supernal will it; that a single word can provide a lifetime of every kind of jewel and every kind of wonder. too much sweetness makes one sick. it is better to study and delight at the most leisurely place and know each thing you encounter than to act with too much hunger to regurgitate that there was no chance for rumination and all the produce has been stripped from the stalks in plague.

i am in the process presently of preventing my eyes from widening and trying to hitch my lips to a post. i am also in the process of learning how to use sefaria's sheets and trying to find a way to get further from moron and closer to moreh

sheets.title: The Different Opinions on Btzelem Elokim
sheets.summary:
At humanity's point of origin, the Torah tells us that Hashem made us "btzelem Elokim," in His image. The significance of this is not lost on us, but the details behind such significance sometimes are. 

Which part of us was made btzelem Elokim? What are the possibilities? How do we practically understand that? 

This source sheet presents four different opinions or "camps" on btzelem Elokim's meaning, and while it is not all-inclusive, the hope is that it close to that.  

(Main credit is to Rav Dovid'll Weinberg for these sources)

If we follow the patterns instead of ignoring them, Genesis may be more coherent than we have been trained to notice.

description.en: God is central in traditional Jewish texts. God [utters the world into existence](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en) from the outset of Genesis, and Rambam, in the opening to his halakhic masterpiece, Mishnah Torah, explains that belief in God is the [foundation of all foundations](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishneh_Torah%2C_Foundations_of_the_Torah.1.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Countless Jewish sources discuss God's essence, the constraints of using human language to describe a transcendent Being, and how people are to develop relationships with God.

*Sheratzim* are small creatures that creep or crawl, described and listed in Leviticus [11:29-30](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.11.31?ven=Tanakh:_The_Holy_Scriptures,_published_by_JPS&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Their corpses convey impurity to people and vessels when encountered in specific ways.

The sun plays a central role in Jewish texts as a physical source of light, a regulator of ritual time, and a symbol of radiance, strength, and divine order. In the Bible, it is created on the fourth day of creation and features in key narratives such as Joseph's [dream](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.37.9?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) and the miracle of Joshua halting the sun, as well as in poetic [metaphors](https://www.sefaria.org/Judges.5.31?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Rabbinic literature ties practices like daily prayer to sunrise and sunset and discusses the sun's role in structuring the calendar. Liturgical [texts](https://www.sefaria.org/Siddur_Sefard%2C_Shabbat_Morning_Services%2C_Shema_%26_Blessings.4?ven=hebrew|Torat_Emet_357&lang=bi) praise God for continually renewing creation and bringing forth the sun each day, and Jewish philosophical works develop the sun as a symbol of divine constancy.

The first people, Adam and Eve, eat from the Tree of Knowledge and are then banished from the Garden of Eden. Their elder son, Cain, kills their younger son, Abel, and Cain is destined to a life of wandering.
description.he: פרשת בראשית, הפרשה הראשונה בתורה, מתארת את ראשיתו של העולם. אלוהים בורא את העולם בשישה ימים ונח ביום השביעי. הוא מניח את האדם בגן עדן ומצווה עליו ליהנות מפירות הגן מלבד מפרי עץ הדעת. בעצת הנחש חוה ואדם אוכלים מעץ הדעת, ולכן מגורשים מגן עדן. בנם הבכור קין הורג את אחיו הצעיר הבל, וקין נידון להיות נע ונד בארץ.

description.en: As part of creation, humans are charged with the protection of trees. Those trees that produce fruit in the land of Israel are subject to the various Torah regulations regarding Temple gifts and tithes. Trees are also likened to the Torah itself and serve as a popular metaphor in Jewish tradition.
description.he: בהיותם חלק מהבריאה, בני האדם מופקדים בהגנת ושמירת העצים. בתורה יש מצוות שונות החלות על עצי פרי בארץ ישראל כמו תרומות ומעשרות והבאת ביכורים למקדש. העץ הוא דימוי נפוץ במסורת היהודית לתורה עצמה וכן למי שמקיים אותה.

description.en: Birds feature in the Jewish textual tradition from the opening chapter of the Torah, which [recounts](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.21?lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) how birds were created on the fifth day of creation. [Noah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/noah?tab=admin) uses birds to help determine whether it is safe to leave the ark, and other parts of the Torah discuss laws surrounding birds, like which ones are prohibited for consumption and the obligation to send away a mother bird before taking her young. Later Jewish texts expand on these concepts and other aspects of the nature and qualities of birds.

en.title: A Verse Calls Out to Us
en.prompt: About the first verse of the Torah, the renowned 11th-century commentator Rashi says, “This verse says nothing but ‘interpret me (with midrash)!'” Ramban, a scholar of 13th-century Spain, discusses the midrashim that Rashi quotes.

description.en: The term “midrash” refers both to a process of elaborative interpretation and to a [body of literature](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Midrash) that is made up of midrashic interpretations of the Tanakh, mostly compiled from the third century CE through the middle ages. Midrashim (plural of midrash) are sometimes categorized into halakhic midrash, which derives legal conclusions from biblical verses, and aggadic midrash, which interprets verses for anything non-legal, especially narrative elaborations and ethical teachings. Many works of midrash combine both categories, and sections of midrash also appear frequently throughout the [Talmud](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Talmud/Bavli).

description.he: על פי התלמוד, מאז ימי אדם הראשון ועד נֹח נהגה האנושות בצמחונות. במקורות יהודיים אחרים מלמדים כי ההיתר לאכול בשר שניתן לבסוף מידי אלוהים היה פשרה מוסרית בלבד, ועל כן ההלכה מגבילה את סוגי הבשר המותרים לאכילה ואת הדרכים המותרות לאכילתו.
description.en: According to the Talmud, from Adam to Noah humans practiced vegetarianism (tzimchonut). In the Jewish sources, God's eventual permission to eat meat is often seen as nothing more than an ethical compromise and Jewish law restricts the type and way that meat is eaten.

description.en: The Hebrew word “kabbalah” means “receiving,” and it has multiple specific associations in different contexts. It is often used to refer to a “received” tradition, passed down through generations. In particular in classic rabbinic sources it refers to the [Prophets](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Tanakh/Prophets) and the [Writings](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Tanakh/Writings), the parts of the [Hebrew Bible](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Tanakh) other than the five books of the Torah. Nowadays, it is most often used to refer to [Jewish mysticism](https://www.sefaria.org/texts/Kabbalah), and sometimes to a particular school of Jewish mysticism that began in Western Europe in the middle ages and spread and evolved throughout the Jewish world.

Life is a fundamental value in Jewish texts. This value influences legal decisions, including end-of-life choices and when one is permitted to transgress other laws like Shabbat observance. The value placed on life raises questions about the meaning of life and how one should live one’s life, of which there are plentiful discussions in Jewish texts.

Animals feature in a variety of contexts, such as biblical and talmudic stories, legal discussions about how to treat them, and poetic liturgical works that marvel at their wonders.

Time is a concept that appears from the very beginning of the Torah, as the world's creation unfolds over seven days, each of which is divided into evening and morning. Sources throughout the Jewish textual tradition discuss how God and people sanctify time, different ways of relating to the passing of time, how time governs the performance of commandments, and how to make the most of one's time.

Moshe ben Nachman, also known as Ramban, was a leading Torah scholar of the middle ages who authored commentaries on Torah and the Talmud. He was a posek who wrote responsa and stand-alone works on Halachic topics, as well as works on mysticism, science and philosophy. Ramban's commentary on the Torah often critiques earlier commentaries and incorporates kabbalistic teachings. description.en: The sun plays a central role in Jewish texts as a physical source of light, a regulator of ritual time, and a symbol of radiance, strength, and divine order. In the Bible, it is created on the fourth day of creation and features in key narratives such as Joseph's [dream](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.37.9?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) and the miracle of Joshua halting the sun, as well as in poetic [metaphors](https://www.sefaria.org/Judges.5.31?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Rabbinic literature ties practices like daily prayer to sunrise and sunset and discusses the sun's role in structuring the calendar. Liturgical [texts](https://www.sefaria.org/Siddur_Sefard%2C_Shabbat_Morning_Services%2C_Shema_%26_Blessings.4?ven=hebrew|Torat_Emet_357&lang=bi) praise God for continually renewing creation and bringing forth the sun each day, and Jewish philosophical works develop the sun as a symbol of divine constancy.

description.en: In the opening chapter of the Torah, God creates the moon, alongside other celestial bodies, on the fourth day of creation. In Jewish tradition and practice, the moon plays a central role in determining the calendar: New Hebrew months start with the appearance of new moons, which also lead to the determination of holiday dates. Texts throughout the ages discuss the moon's symbolism and significance; halakhic practices related to the moon, like the concept of blessing the new moon; and ways in which the lunar calendar interacts with the solar calendar.

The opening chapter of the Torah [describes](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.11?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) how God created plants, trees, and vegetation on the third day of creation. Jewish law includes many commandments related to plants and agriculture, such as leaving the corners of fields for the poor ([*peah*](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.19.9?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)), observing the sabbatical year ([*shemittah*](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/shemitah?tab=admin)), and refraining from eating a tree's fruit during its first three years ([*orlah*](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.19.23?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en)). The Prophets and works of Jewish thought frequently use plants as metaphors – like in the [comparison](https://www.sefaria.org/Jeremiah.17.8?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) of righteous people to flourishing trees planted by water – and as symbols of life, growth, and God's ongoing care for creation.

Birds feature in the Jewish textual tradition from the opening chapter of the Torah, which [recounts](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.21?lang=he&with=all&lang2=he) how birds were created on the fifth day of creation. [Noah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/noah?tab=admin) uses birds to help determine whether it is safe to leave the ark, and other parts of the Torah discuss laws surrounding birds, like which ones are prohibited for consumption and the obligation to send away a mother bird before taking her young. Later Jewish texts expand on these concepts and other aspects of the nature and qualities of birds.

The plague of wild animals is the fourth of ten plagues that God wrought upon the Egyptians when Pharoah refused to let the enslaved Israelites go. It is described in [Exodus 8:16-28](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus.8.16?lang=he&with=all&lang2=he)

description.en: The opening two [chapters](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=he) of the Torah describe how God created the world in six days and rested on the seventh. These chapters are some of the most analyzed words in the Jewish textual tradition and serve as a basis for discussions of topics like [human dignity](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/human-dignity?tab=admin), God's role in the world, Shabbat, and humankind's responsibility for continuing the creation process and caring for the world.

Angels – often understood as messengers of God or supernatural beings – appear widely throughout Tanakh, rabbinic literature, kabbalistic literature, and Jewish liturgy. In the Torah, they often convey messages, like when an angel [informs Hagar](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.16.7?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) that she will give birth to a son, or when an angel [tells Abraham](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.22.11?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) not to sacrifice Isaac. In the books of the Prophets, angels are also featured as part of visions and prophecies. Later Jewish texts expand on the nature of angels, describing the roles and attributes of specific angels and how the belief in angels shapes certain Jewish [practices](https://www.sefaria.org/Shalom_Aleichem.1?lang=bi).

Wind plays a role from the very beginning of the Torah, as a [wind from God](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.2?lang=bi&vside=The_Contemporary_Torah,_Jewish_Publication_Society,_2006|en&with=Translation%20Open&lang2=en) sweeps over the waters in the opening verses of Genesis. Winds are critical in other prominent biblical stories as well, such as when the wind helps split the Red Sea, brings [quail](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.11.31?lang=bi&aliyot=0) to the desert, or helps revive the dead in Ezekiel's [Valley of Dry Bones prophecy](https://www.sefaria.org/Ezekiel.37.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). In rabbinic texts, the rabbis discuss how wind affects areas of halakhah, such as under what conditions someone is [liable for damages](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Bava_Kamma.60a.4?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) caused by wind and what types of wind the [sukkah walls](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Sukkah.23a.4?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) must withstand. The word "wind" is also used in the context of the directions north, east, south, and west and their spiritual significance, as well as to refer to a person's [spirit](https://www.sefaria.org.il/Pirkei_Avot.4.4?ven=hebrew|Torat_Emet_357&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) or a moral force.
